194 THIRTY-SECOND REPORT U. S. CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 
April 23, 1915. 
Fred Gilmore, of the District of Columbia, and Robert Taylor, of the District of Columbia, unclassified laborers at $660 per annum in the Post Office Department, may be appointed classified laborers at $660 per annum in the same department without reference to civil-service rules. The above order was issued on request of the Postmaster General, who stated that these men were highly desirable as messengers, entirely trustworthy, and had rendered excellent service, having been directly connected with the office of the Postmaster General since the beginning of the present administration. 
April 27, 1915. 
Mr. Charles W. G. Brett may be transferred from the position of mechanician at 
$1,200 per annum to a clerkship at the same salary, in the Bureau of the Census, Department of Commerce, without reference to the civil-service rules. Mr. Brett was appointed as mechanician on September 16, 1908. On March 19, 1912, he met with an accident, in the line of duty, which resulted in the loss of his left eye. His transfer to the clerical rollisrecommended by the Director of the Census, who states that Mr. Brett’s experience in connection with the various machines used in the bureau, his familiarity with the matter to be tabulated, and his general educa- tion are believed to be such as to fit him for clerical duties, and that his services have always been satisfactory. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation. 
April 27, 1915. 
Mrs. Lillian B. S. Grant may be reinstated to a position in the classified service in the Post Office Department without regard to the length of time she has been sep- arated from the service. Mrs. Grant, as Mrs. Lillie B. Silcott, was appointed to the position of printer’s assistant in the Bureau of Printing and Engraving on August 2, 1895, and was pro- moted to operative and through the several grades of that position. On July 1, 1902, she was transferred to the Post Office Department as clerk at $900, and was promoted to $1,000 July 1, 1905. She resigned May 9, 1912. 
The Postmaster General advises that it is stated that Mrs. Grant’s husband is a ermanent invalid, and that she is therefore compelled to provide a livelihood for Poth her husband and herself. In view of the circumstances and the fact that the records of the department show that her services were satisfactory and her duties faithfully discharged, the Postmaster General states that no objection would be offered by the department to the reinstatement of Mrs. Grant by Executive order. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend the issuance of an order in this 
case. 
April 27, 1915. 
Mrs. Lucy Jones Harris, of Kentucky, may be appointed to a position in the Immi- gration Service, Department of Labor, without reference to the civil-service rules. This order is issued in view of the statement of the Secretary of Labor that the department can use to advantage the services of Mrs. Harris in the Immigration Service, in which the Commissioner General of Immigration informs him there is urgent need 
of a woman of Mrs. Harris’s peculiar qualifications in the labor distribution branch of the service at New York City, where it is deemed advisable, in the development of this new service, to have a woman of her high character and sympathetic initiative, who is able at once to take care of the Teqiiremanis of the woman labor problem and greatly assist in carrying out the plan of distribution inauguarted by the department. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend the issuance of an order in this case. 
May 4, 1915. 
Mr. William Leroy Fairbanks may be transferred from chief clerk of the American Embassy at London to a clerkship in the Department of Commerce. He has served since 1908, at first in the State Department, then in the American Legation at Peking, and since 1910 in his present position. The Secretary of Commerce, with the concurrence of the Civil Service Commission, recommends the issuance of this order in view of the special qualifications of Mr. Fairbanks for the work of the Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce. 
May 11, 1915. 
Miss Agnes Deery may be appointed as a nurse in the Indian Service without reference to the requirement of examination under the civil-service rules. . This action, based upon the recommendation of the Secretary of the Interior, is in fulfillment of

EXECUTIVE ORDERS. 125 
an agreement between representatives of the Departments of the Interior and War in October, 1912, when it was understood that Miss Deery was eligible for transfer. Miss Deery served from June 12, 1902, to May 7, 1914, at the Apache Indian Hos- pital at Fort Sill, Okla., with distinguished faithfulness and success in the positions 
of matron and nurse. The Apache prisoners having been removed to the Mescalero Agency, N. Mex., it is desired to appoint Miss Deery as nurse in the Indian Service. The Civil Service Commission concurs in the recommendation for this order. 
May 11, 1915. 
Mrs. Enna Wilson Noel may be reinstated to a position in the classified service in the War Department without regard to the requirements of the civil service rules. Mrs. Noel is the widow of Edward McC. Noel, whose death on April 16, 1915, termi￾nated a service of nearly 33 years in the office of the Surgeon General, and leaves her dependent upon employment for support. Prior to her marriage she served as clerk in the office of the Surgeon General from December 18, 1893, to February 9, 1900, and previously in other offices since November 7, 1889. Her reinstatement is recom- mended by the Secretary of War and the Surgeon General of the Army. The Civil ServicesCommission does not concur in the recommendation. 
May 11, 1915. 
Mrs. Laura F. Richmond may be reinstated as an operative in the Bureau of Engraving and Printing without regard to the length of time she has been separated from the service. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Acting Secretary of the Treasury in view of the efficient service rendered by the husband of Mrs. Richmond in the Treasury Department for 28 years, and in view of the fact that Mr. Richmond is now wholly incapacitated both mentally and physically for the performance of duty, and also because of the satisfactory service rendered by Mrs. Richmond while a former employee in the Bureau of Engraving and Printing where she served for a period of 
seven years. 
The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation. 
May 13, 1915. 
Michael L. Eidsness, jr., of Iowa, a minor clerk of class D ($900) in the Post Office Department, may be promoted to the position of clerk without further civil service examination. This order was issued upon the recommendation of the Postmaster General, who stated that while Mr. Eidsness was not able to pass the first-grade examination he had a very exceptional record in the

126 THIRTIETH REPORT OF THE U. S. CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 
A vacancy exists in the Treasury Department to which Mrs. Branan can be appointed. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend the issuance of this order. 
(It should be noted that this Executive order waives the labor regulations and not the civil-service rules.) 
March 3, 1913. 
Thomas Butler of the District of Columbia may be appointed without examination to the position of laborer in the classified civil service. Mr. Butler was appointed four years ago as a messenger in the immediate office of the Postmaster General to one of the several positions in each cabinet officer’s department that are excepted from the usual civil-service requirements. The Postmaster General states that he has proved to be efficient; that he quickly learned the duties of his posi- tion and the run of the department, and that he is conscientious and reliable. The Postmaster General further states that on practical grounds it would be desirable for the department to take advantage of Mr. Butler's four years’ training and continue hin nine service. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in recommending this order. 
March 3, 1913. : 
Col. Heber M. Creel of North Dakota may be appointed a supervisor of Indian schools without regard to the civil-service rules. His education at the United States Military Academy, his military experience during many years in the West, and present physical condition qualify him for the duties of such supervisor. The Secretary of the Interior recommends the issuance of this order. The Civil Service Commission, however, disapproves it. 
March 3, 1913. 
Mr. H. Norman Fleming may be reinstated as a clerk in the Pension Office without regard to the civil-service rule fixing one year as the period of eligibility. 
Mr. Fleming was appointed copyist at $720 in the Pension Office September 26, 1882; three times promoted, and resigned December 31, 1906. This order is recommended by the Commissioner of Pensions, but is not concurred in by the Civil Service Commission. 
March 3, 1913. 
Joab P. Foster may be reinstated as a veterinary inspector in the Department of Agriculture. Mr. Foster was appointed on May 16, 1908, through the veterinary inspector exami- nation, as an inspector at $1,400 per annum, and served in that capacity until October 14, 1910, when he was granted leave of absence without pay on account of ill health. He continued on leave of absence without pay until December 31, 1910, when his appointment was terminated. It appears that he has fully regained his health and is 
in proper condition to resume his duties. Because of his past experience in Federal and State live-stock work, the Secretary of Agriculture states that as the services of Mr. Foster would be of especial value to the department, his reinstatement would be distinctly in the interest of good administration. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend the issuance of this order. 
March 3, 1913. 
Mrs. Katharine T. Gerald may be appointed to a classified position in the Bureau of Pensions without examination. Mrs. Gerald was appointed on the temporary roll of the Bureau of Pensions on August 28, 1912, the appointment being limited to 60 days, and owing to her good record the appointment was extended October 28, 1912, until further notice. The Civil i Commission does not recommend the issuance of this order. 
March 3, 1913. 
Miss Alice E. Gibbs may be appointed to a classified position in the Government service without compliance with the civil-service rules. WoT Miss Gibbs has had extensive experience as a stenographer and typewriter in private employ and at the Capitol, where she has been employed for the past seven years in a secretarial capacity, and has proven herself to be exceptionally competent and trust￾worthy. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend the issuance of this order. 
March 3, 1913. 
Mr. Edward Hawkins may be appointed a laborer in the Department of Agriculture without reference to the civil-service rules. : Mr. Hawkins is now on temporary duty in the Department of Agriculture, perform- ing emergency work. He was previously employed for four years by the Commis-

EXECUTIVE ORDERS. 127 
sioners of the District of Columbia and bears an excellent testimonial. The Depart- ment of Agriculture reports that the department ‘would be glad to place him in the department, as he is a clean, reliable sort of man.” The Civil Service Commission does not recommend the issuance of this order. 
March 3, 1913. 
Mr. Fred Roege may be reinstated as assistant postmaster in the post office at Pen- sacola, Fla., without regard to the length of time that he has been separated from the service. Mr. Roege was appointed to the classified service on August 28, 1900, and served con￾tinuously till July 13, 1911, when he resigned. He held the position of clerk in the Treasury Department, money-order clerk in the Washington post office, and post- office inspector. He made application for reinstatement within the year of his eligi￾bility, but was misinformed to the effect that his military service and honorable discharge therefrom rendered him eligible for reinstatement at any time under the rules. In view of the fact that he was misinformed as to his rights of reinstatement the com- mission concurs in the recommendation of the Postmaster General, the First Assistant Postmaster General, and the postmaster at Pensacola that he be reinstated by ex- ecutive order. 
March 3, 1913. 
Mr. Charles H. Shaw, now employed in the Customs Service at the port of New York, may be appointed to a classified position in the New York customs service without reference to the civil-service rules. This appointment is recommended by the collector of the port of New York and the Secretary of the Treasury, but is not concurred in by the Civil Service Commission. It appears from the papers in the case that Mr. Shaw who is a lawyer, had been employed from July 1, 1909, in the customhouse in an unclassified position on the “fraud roll;” that he had rendered most excellent service, and that the collector recommended the order as one distinctly in the interests of the service. 
March 3, 1913. 
Mr. Jesse L. Suter may be appointed to a clerical position in the classified service without reference to the civil-service rules. Mr. Suter was appointed confidential clerk at $1,800 per annum in the office of the First Assistant Postmaster General on August 9, 1909, the position being excepted from examination under Schedule A of the civil-service rules. The Postmaster Gen- eral states that Mr. Suter, since his appointment, has qualified himself in an excep- tional manner for use

EXECUTIVE ORDERS. 123 
Dr. Beverley’s reinstatement by Executive order is recommended by Gen. George W. Goethals, Governor of the Panama Canal. Dr. Beverley entered the service on July 6, 1904; served through the period when tropical diseases were prevalent, and by his efficient service was successively promoted until he held one of the highest positions therein at the close of his service December 15, 1913, being rated as ‘‘excel- lent” in both conduct and character of work. Necessity for a change of climate required his resignation, but he has recovered from the effects of his long residence in the Tropics and desires to return to work on the Isthmus. 
The Civil Service Commission concurs in recommending this order. 
March 23, 1915. 
Edward D. White may be reinstated as a letter carrier in the Oakland, Cal., post office without regard to the length of time he has been separated from the service. He was appointed substitute carrier in the Oakland office on September 1, 1902; was made a regular carrier on October 1, 1903, and served until January 31, 1913. The Postmaster General states that as Mr. White is intelligent and was a very competent and faithful employee while in the service, the department will not interpose any objection to his reinstatement in the service. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend the issuance of this order. 
April 6, 1915. 
Mr. John D. Campbell may be reinstated to a position in the Railway Mail Service without regard to the length of time he has been separated from the service. Mr. Campbell was appointed a clerk in the Railway Mail Service on October 29, 1887, classified with that service on May 1, 1889, as a clerk at $1,000 per annum, and resigned November 3, 1902, on account of his impaired physical condition. Itappears that he has now fully recovered his health. The Postmaster General states that his 
services were satisfactory to the department during his 15 years’ service and that the department will interpose no objection to his reinstatement through the issuance of an Executive order. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend this order. 
April 13, 1915. : 
Mrs. Eleanor S. Ramsay may be transferred from the position of office helper in the Government Printing Office to a clerical position in the Navy Department without reference to the civil-service rules. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of the Navy, who states that Mrs. Ramsay has a very good record for efficiency in the Government Printing Office, and, after investigation, he is satisfied that she is competent to per- form satisfactorily clerical duties in the Navy Department. Mrs. Ramsay was appointed a gold worker in the Government Printing Office, September 28, 1903, and since Sobtember 20, 1907, has been continuously employed as an office helper at 35 cents per hour. ; The Civil Service Commission does not concur in recommending this order. 
April 17, 1915. 
Samuel Z. C. Westerfield, of Nebraska, now a messenger with the British Arbitra- tion Claims Commission, may be appointed without examination to an assistant messengership in the Department of State. The position now filled by Mr. Wester- field is abolished by legislation effective July 1, and because of his efficiency it is 
deemed in the interest of the public service to continue him in the employ of the Department of State. 
April 21, 1915. 
Mr. Arthur S. Kellom, formerly a letter carrier at the Chico, Cal., post office, may be reinstated in the postal service without regard to the length of time he has been separated from the service. ‘he reinstatement of Mr. Kellom is recommended by the Postmaster General, who states that a careful review of the papers in this case discloses that the charges on which the carrier was removed were not wholly true and that the action taken by the department was based upon statements which for the most part are not borne out by facts recently developed and were the result of prejudice on the part of the former ostmaster and, possibly, the post-office inspector who conducted the case, and it 18 believed that an injustice was done and that the offenses charged against Carrier Eolloms even if true, were not such as to justify so severe a punishment as that inflicted.

152 FORTIETH REPORT U. S. CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 
WAIVER OF EXAMINATION REQUIREMENT. May 7, 1923. 
The Executive order of May 10, 1921, requiring candidates to take civil service examinations for presidential postmasterships, is hereby waived so as to permit the appointment of Henry M. Stowe to the position of postmaster at Bedford, Va., without 
examination. 
May 7, 1928. 
The Executive order of May 10, 1921, prescribing examinations of applicants for presidential postmasters is hereby waived in so far as it applies to the case of the ostmaster at Falmouth, Mass., in order to permit the reappointment without exam￾ination of George W. Jones. Mr. Jones was appointed postmaster in the Falmouth, Mass., post office October 12, 1889, and has been serving continuously in that capacity since that time. The Civil Service Commission concurs in this recommendation. 
REAPPOINTMENT WITHOUT EXAMINATION. 
WAIVER OF AGE LIMIT. May 11, 1928. 
That part of the Executive order of May 10, 1921, which pertains to the age limit of candidates for the presidential postmastership examinations is hereby waived so as to permit the examination papers of Isaac I. Bargen, candidate for the position of Postimasior at Mountain Lake, Minn., to be rated by the Civil Service Commission. 
e has served as postmaster since 1902. The Civil Service Commission concurs in recommending this order. 
May 18, 1923. 
That part of the Executive order of May 10, 1921, which pertains to the age limit of candidates for the presidential postmastership examination is hereby waived so as to permit the examination papers of W. W. Copeland, candidate for the position of postmaster at Burlington, Iowa, to be rated by the Civil Service Commission. 
May 28, 1928. 
The papers of the examination of Mr. George W. Sisler for postmaster at Stanwood, lowa, may be rated by the Civil Service Commission, waiving the age limit. Mr. Sisler was postmaster from 1911 to 1917. It is stated that he is at the present time the choice of the majority, if not all, of the business men of the town for the office and that he is very competent. The Civil Service Commission concurs with the Postmaster General in recommend- ing the issuance of this order. 
MISCELLANEOUS ORDER. 
AMENDMENT OF EXECUTIVE ORDER OF JANUARY 17, 1873, PROHIBITING THE HOLDING 
OF FEDERAL AND STATE OFFICES AT THE SAME TIME, 
January 2, 1923. 
The Executive order of January 17, 1873, prohibiting the holding of Federal and State offices at the same time is hereby amended so as to permit the appointment as special agents of persons holding State, territorial, or municipal positions when such action is deemed necessary by the Secretary of Labor to secure a more efficient admin- istration of any law coming within the purview of the Department of Labor. 
ELIGIBILITY FOR REENTRANCE TO THE CLASSIFIED SERVICE FOR A PERIOD OF FIVE 
YEARS FROM MARCH 31, 1922, OF CERTAIN PERSONS SEPARATED FROM THE BUREAU 
OF ENGRAVING AND PRINTING. 
February 14, 1923. 
The following-named persons who were separated from the Bureau of Engraving and Printing are eligible to reenter any part of the classified service in appropriate positions for a period of five years from March 31, 1922, on certificate of the Civil Service Commission: P. J. Farrell, James M. Fisher, George E. Jacobs, Thomas F. Roche, George U. Rose, Adam P. Ruth, Thomas F. Slattery, E. H. Ashworth, Jesse Benjamin, Ralph H. Onappell George C. Cole, William C. Deane, John J. Deviny, B. R. Stickney, Norman Underwood, H. I. Wilson, Benjamin Goldsworthy.

EXEMPTING POSITION OF SHIPPING COMMISSIONER FROM CIVIL-SERVICE REGULATION. 
March 15, 19283. 
The position of{ShippingiCommissioner at the several ports of the United States is hereby exempted from civil-service regulation. Officers of the jNaval Reserve force who bear recommendations from the Secretary of the Navy shall be given priority whenever it is necessary to select new men to these positions. 
POSITIONS OF GUARD IN THE OFFICE OF ,THE SUPERINTENDENT, STATE, WAR, AND NAVY DEPARTMENT BUILDINGS. June 2, 1923. 
Positions of guard in the office of the superintendent, State, War, and Navy Depart» ment Buildings, may, during the remainder of the fiscal year 1923 and during the fiscal year 1924, be filled by the superintendent without compliance with the civil- service law and rules when filled by suitably qualified retired enlisted men from the Army, Navy, or Marine Corps, or retired firemen or policemen of the District of Columbia Government who have been retired therefrom under honorable conditions. The excessive turnover in the guard force, due to inadequate salaries under exist- ing conditions, and the desirability of assigning to the temporary frame buildings as guards men who have had training and experience in the Fire Department indicate the desirability of the exception proposed. It is anticipated that the reclassifica- Hon fel; which becomes effective oo 1, 1924, will take care of the situation after 
at date. 
The Civil Service Commission concurs with the Secretary of State and the Acting Secretaries of War and Navy in recommending this order. 
PERMISSION TO EMPLOYEES LIVING IN BRENTWOOD, MD., TO BECOME CANDIDATES FOR OR HOLD MUNICIPAL OFFICE, June 7, 1923. 
The Executive order of February 14, 1912, as subsequently amended, permitting employees in the executive civil service permanently residing in certain incor- porated municipalities adjacent to the District of Columbia to become candidates for or hold municipal office therein, is hereby further amended so as to include the in- corporated municipality of Brentwood, Md., among those named in the order. thereof the following words: “and of Pomology;” so that as amended the paragraph
will read:
(/) Chiefs of divisions, except in the Department of Agriculture the chiefs of
the following divisions: Entomology, economic ornithology and mammalogy, and
pomology.
Special Departmental Rule No. 1.
Special departmental rule No. 1 is hereby amended by dropping from among the
places therein excepted from examination the following:
In the Department of Agriculture, office of Secretary: The assistant chief of the
Division of Pomology.
Approved November 2, 1894.
Grover Cleveland.
AMENDMENT TO SPECIAL DEPARTMENTAL RULE No. 1.
Special departmental rule No. 1 is hereby amended by adding to the places
therein excepted from examination in the Department of the Treasury the following:
In the Bureau of Statistics: One expert in mechanical designs and in diagraming
commercial and financial facts.
Approved November 2, 1894.
Grover Cleveland.
AMENDMENT TO DEPARTMENTAL RULE VII.
Departmental Rule VII, clause 1, is hereby amended by inserting at the end of
line six the following:
Vacancies in places authorized to be filled by noncompetitive examination may be
filled without examination, for a period not exceeding thirty days, until a regular
appointment can be made upon certification by the Commission.
Every such appointment, and the reasons therefor, shall be at once reported to the
Commission.
Approved.
Grover Cleveland.

134 TWENTY-FIFTH REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION.
July 2, 1908.
Mr. Joe M. Johnson may be reinstated in the Government Printing Office
without regard to the length of his separation therefrom.
Mr. Johnson served continuously in the Government Printing Office as a com¬
positor and proof reader from February 7, 1899, to November 20, 1905, and
inasmuch as he had been separated from the service for more than one year the
commission was without authority to issue a certificate for his reinstatement.
The Public Printer stated that Mr. Johnson is thoroughly familiar with the
work of the office and he believed that his reinstatement would be in the inter¬
ests of the service rather than to try out new material, as the office was not at
that time as well supplied with talent in his line as the Public Printer wished
it to be.
July 16, 1908.
Mr. Herman Gluck, whose services as a deputy collector of internal revenue at
New York were discontinued on March 1, 1907, may be reinstated without regard
to the expiration of his year of eligibility.
Mr. Gluck served as deputy collector in the third internal revenue district of
New York from September 16, 1905, until March 1, 1907, when he was dropped
without prejudice because of his disappearance from home. The Commissioner
of Internal Revenue stated that although Mr. Gluck had been separated from
the service for more than one year the office in which he worked had been
notified before the expiration of the year that application would be made for
reinstatement, but no formal action was taken by that office within the year
limitation. The Commissioner of Internal Revenue also stated that inasmuch
as Mr. Gluck instituted proceedings looking toward his reinstatement within
the year limit he should not suffer a hardship because of circumstances over
which he had no control. The commission not having power to issue a certifi¬
cate of reinstatement after the expiration of the limitation fixed by the rules,
an executive order was necessary for the reinstatement of Mr. Gluck.
July 16, 1908.
George Terwilliger may be reinstated in the Government Printing Office
without regard to the length of his separation from the service.
Mr. Terwilliger served as compositor in the Government Printing Office from
August 14, 1894, to March 5, 1897, when he resigned. The Public Printer, in a
letter to the President recommending his reinstatement, stated that since his
resignation Mr. Terwilliger has frequently been employed as a temporary com¬
positor, and his service has been highly satisfactory and his record first class.
The Public Printer also stated that he had personal knowledge of Mr. Terwil￾liger’s ability and efficiency, and that inasmuch as he was perfectly familiar
with the work of the Government Printing Office his reinstatement would be
in the interest of the service.
July 16, 1908.
W. S. Lowe, Grosvenor A. Porter, T. E. Brentz, and E. E. Kinnett, of Okla¬
homa, may be appointed without reference to the civil-service rules as experts
in the suppression of the liquor traffic among the Indians.
Mr. William E. Johnson, special officer in charge of the suppression of the
liquor traffic on several Indian reservations, in a letter to the Commissioner of
Indian Affairs, made the following statement in regard to these positions:
The essential qualifications for an officer in this service are honesty, industry,
personal courage, and tact. I can not see how a civil-service examination can
ascertain these qualifications in an applicant. I am very anxious to eliminate
this matter of killing and being killed, which was a factor in my work in the
Indian Territory. The men who were killed down there were all compara-

soned men were more able to travel the gait I set for them without these trage¬
dies. For this reason above mentioned, it seems to me to be wise to select as
these four deputies men who are of proved ability and who were conspicuous
in making our efforts a success in the Indian Territory during the past year and
a half.
The Acting Commissioner of Indian Affairs concurred in the recommendation
of Mr. Johnson, and the commission also believed that it was impractical to
fill these positions through examination. The persons appointed as experts
have all had considerable experience specially fitting them for this work. W. S.
Lowe has had a long carreer in the Indian Territory as deputy United States
marshal, railway detective, and deputy. Grosvenor A. Porter has been United
States marshal for several years in the Indian Territory. T. E. Brentz has a
long record as deputy United States marshal in the Indian Territory, and has
been conspicuous in the warfare against boot leggers. E. E. Kinnett has had
several years’ experience as deputy marshal, bailiff, etc., in the western dis¬
trict of Oklahoma.
July 18, 1908.
Mr. William E. Shields may be reinstated in the Government Printing Office
without regard to the length of his separation from the office.
Mr. Shields was appointed as a proof reader in the Government Printing
Office April 5, 1893, and resigned April 9, 1907. The Public Printer, in a letter
to the President, stated that his services in that office were satisfactory in
every detail and his record first class. Since leaving the Government Printing
Office Mr. Shields has had charge of the proof reading on several of the large
newspapers of the country, and at the time of the issuance of the order was
chief proof reader in the office of the Baltimore Sun. The Public Printer also
stated that the proof reading of his office must be improved, and he knew of
no better way to accomplish that end than to secure men who were willing to
resign good positions elsewhere. The President, in a letter to the commission,
stated that from his personal knowledge that branch of the Government Print¬
ing Office needed improvement, and for that reason he issued the above order.

REPORT OF UNITED STATES CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 139 
The opinion of the President conveyed in the letter of his Secretary will be treated as an Executive order. (Minute 1, Mar. 23, 1912.) 
PETITIONS TO CONGRESS BY CIVIL-SERVICE EMPLOYEES, 
April 8, 1912.1 
It is hereby ordered that petitions or other communications regarding public busi- ness addressed to Congress or either House or any committee or Member thereof by officers or employees in the civil service of the United States shall be transmitted through the heads of their respective departments or offices, who shall forward them without delay with such comment as they may deem requisite in the public interest. Officers and employees are strictly prohibited either directly or indirectly from at- tempting to secure legislation, or to influence pending legislation, except in the manner above prescribed. This order supersedes the Executive orders of January 31, 1902, January 25, 1906, and November 26, 1909, regarding the same general matter 
EXCEPTIONS IN MACHINE SHOP OF THE BUREAU OF THE CENSUS. 
August 21, 1812. - 
With a view to meeting emergencies in the machine shop of the Bureau of the Census, in connection with the continuation of the Thirteenth Decennial Census work during the fiscal year 1913, the Secretary of Commerce and Labor is hereby authorized to employ, until June 30, 1913, without reference to the civil-service rules, such machinists, toolmakers, electricians, and apprentice boys (machinists) as may be necessary for the prosecution of the work whenever, in his opinion, it is not prac- ticable to make such appointments from the civil-service lists. This order extends the authority for similar appointments contained in the Executive order of December 29, 1909. The Civil Service Commission concurs with the department in recommending this order, in view of the representations of the department as to its necessity. ! 
EMPLOYMENT IN PENSION OFFICE OF FORMER TREASURY EMPLOYEES. 
August 24, 1912. 
The Commissioner of Pensions is directed to employ as extra clerks under the appro- priation of $300,000 carried in the sundry civil act approved August 24, 1912, the 30 persons heretofore employed in the office of the Auditor for the Post Office Depart- ment whose names are on the list furnished to the President in a letter of the Secre- tary of the Treasury dated August 22, 1912, said appropriation act authorizing the Commissioner of Pensions to employ clerks heretofore employed in other departments of the Government service. All of these persons except one have a competitive classified status and will be eligible for reinstatement in the Treasury Department under the civil-service rules. 
MODERATOR OF A TOWN MEETING MAY BE A CLASSIFIED EMPLOYEE, 
August 24, 1912. 
The temporary office of moderator of a town meeting and offices of a like character are hereby excepted from the operation of the Executive order of January 17, 1873, prohibiting persons in the Federal civil service from holding office under the charter or ordinances of any municipal corporation, and may be held by persons in the execu- tive civil service. Membership in the civil service ought not to prevent an employee from taking part in the ordinary municipal affairs of the community in which he lives, where that part does not involve permanent service but only such a temporary duty as that of acting as chairman of a municipal business meeting, where such service is not compensated by any salary or other emolument, and where the attention required by such service does not interfere with the regular and efficient discharge of the duties of the Federal office held. In the exercise of the privilege granted by this order officers and employees must not neglect their official duties and must not engage in national, State, or county political activity in violation of the civil-service rules; and in seeking the local offices named or in performing the duties thereof employees shall not use the authority or influence of their Federal positions nor take an active part in political management or 
 
in political campaigns.

CLASSIFICATION OF POSITION OF SPECIAL EMPLOYEE, INTERNAL-REVENUE SERVICE. 
August 24, 1912. 
The position of special employee in the Internal-Revenue Service shall hereafter be regarded as classified under the civil-service act and rules. No such special employee now serving shall be regarded as classified hereunder or shall acquire any right of promotion or transfer under the rules unless he is specially commended therefor by the Commissioner of Internal Revenue, with the approval of the Secretary of the Treasury, because of efficient services rendered, and whose name is embraced in the is furnished to the Civil Service Commission by the Treasury Department of this 
ate. The Treasury Department may make appointments of special employees for a period not exceeding 30 days or not exceeding 45 days in any one quarter of any fiscal year without reference to the civil-service rules. This order shall take effect October 1, 1912, and is issued with the concurrence of the Secretary of the Treasury and the Civil Service Commission. 
CLASSIFICATION AUTHORIZED OF CERTAIN EXPERTS IN THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRI- CULTURE. August 26, 1912. 
Not exceeding 115 persons appointed as experts and agents without examination under Subdivision IX, section 1 of Schedule A, of the civil-service rules, and who now are engaged upon work similar to that of competitive employees, and who are especially recommended by the Secretary of Agriculture because of their proved capacity for efficient service may be transferred to appropriate competitive positions in the Department of Agriculture. By Executive order of this date the provision of the civil-service rules permitting the appointment of agents and experts of the Department of Agriculture without examination is amended to fix more definitely the conditions under which appoint- ments can be made. This order will thus permit the classification of efficient em- ployees who can not be properly regarded as agents or experts under the amended procedure. Many of these persons are college graduates and, having been appointed at a time when agricultural colleges had not developed courses of study along certain technical lines pursued by the department, have become technologists and experts while engaged in the work of the department. The Civil Service Commission recommends this order.

April 22,1912. 
Having considered the written arguments for and against the application for rein- statement of Charles H. Quackenbush in the Railway Mail Service, and having 
reached a conclusion that the offense for which Mr. Quackenbush was removed does not merit more of a penalty than a suspension without pay for a year, and that such penalty has been satisfied, I hereby direct that Mr. Quackenbush may be reinstated in the Railway Mail Service without reference to the provisions of the civil-service rule governing reinstatements. This order 1s made without the approval or disapproval of the Civil Service Com- mission and against the recommendation of the Postmaster General. 
April 30, 1912. 
Commander Homer C. Poundstone, United States Navy, retired, may be employed on the rolls of the United States Civil Service Commission without examination under the civil-service rules. This action is taken at the request of the Civil Service Commission because of his peculiar and exceptional qualifications and his high and recognized attainments. 
May 10, 1912. 
Miss Louise Lester may be appointed a clerk in the classified executive civil service without compliance with the civil-service rules. This order is issued for the reason that it is recommended by the Secretary of the Treasury so that Miss Lester may be appointed a special witness of the destruction of United States securities in the Treasury Department, it being the Secretary’s judgment that Miss Lester possesses special qualifications which will render her par- ticularly desirable as a member of the destruction committee. 
May 27, 1912. 
Mr. Walter L. Barnum may be reinstated to an appropriate clerical position in the classified service without regard to the length of his separation therefrom. Mr. Barnum resigned from the competitive position of clerk in the Post Office Department on February 19, 1908. Since that time he has oso the examination in stenography and typewriting with a high grade, and has eveloped the qualifica- tions of an expert clerk during his service in an excepted position in the Post Office Department from April 1, 1909, to the present time. In view of his high rating and his record as an expert clerk, the commission joins with the Postmaster General in recommending the order. 
May 28, 1912. 
Mr. Wesley M. Featherly, a deputy collector of customs in the Key West, Fla., district from January 1, 1898, to August 21, 1899, when he resigned, may be reinstated without reference to the year limit of the civil-service rules. 
The Civil Service Commission not being advised of the reasons for excepting Mr. Featherly from the year limitation fixed by the civil-service rules makes no recom- mendation respecting this order. 
June 5, 1912. 
Mr. Arthur S. Blum may be reinstated as photographer in the Forest Service, Washington, D. C., without regard to the length of his separation from the service. The Civil Service Commission joins the Secretary of Agriculture in recommending this order because of the unfair treatment received by Mr. Blum through the mis- statements of his superior officer, who has since been adjudged insane. 
June 6, 1912. 
Mrs. Margaret A. Hampton, a clerk at $1,000 per annum on the temporary force of the Thirteenth Census, may be appointed as a clerk at $1,000 per annum in the classified service. 
Mrs. Hampton was appointed through appropriate examination with a rating of 77.45, as a clerk at $600 per annum on the temporary force of the Thirteenth Decennial Census on April 1, 1910, and by successive promotions reached her present rate of $1,000 per annum. She has twice passed the departmental clerk examination. On 
June 24, 1910, while leaving the Census Building, she lost her balance and pitched head first down the full flight of stairs, her skirt having caught on one of the iron plates of the stairs, sustaining injuries which necessitated her absence from the office until July 13 and again from September 30 until December 4. There is grave doubt whether she will ever recover her health, according to statements of several physicians who have attended her. The bureau has endeavored to make all possible restitution but, under existing law, she can not be retained beyond June 30, 1912. Notwith- standing the accident her value as a clerk is above the average.

Mr. Leroy A. McGee may be reinstated to the position of post-office inspector without reference to the time limit upon eligibility for reinstatement.

He has passed the teacher examination, the post-office inspector examination, and the immigrant inspector examination with good ratings. The chief post-office inspector reports that he was a good inspector, that his work was satisfactory, that there is nothing in the files which would be considered against his reinstatement, and that since his resignation Mr. McGee has been practicing law. In view of his good record and the fact that his experience since leaving the service has been such as to increase his efficiency, the Civil Service Commission joins with the Postmaster General in recom- mending the reinstatement,

120 THIRTIETH REPORT OF THE U. S. CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION, 
December 19, 1912. 
Mr. Horace P. DeHart may be transferred from the excepted position of confidential 
clerk to the Assistant Secretary of the Interior to an appropriate competitive position in that department. Mr. DeHart has served continuously as confidential clerk for more than nine years to four assistant secretaries. During that period he has acquired a comprehensive knowledge of the varied business assigned to the assistant secretary, which includes numerous Indian matters, including contracts and bonds, leases, heirship cases, petitions for the approval of sale, etc., appeals in land cases, pension appeals, business 
relating to .eleemosynary institutions, expense and transportation accounts, and many miscellaneous items. His practical experience has made him a useful, efficient and well-trained clerk, and according to the Secretary of the Interior his retention in the service will contribute effectively to the despatch of important business. In view of the proved capacity and exceptional qualifications of Mr. DeHart, the Civil Service Commission joins in the recommendation for his transfer to a competitive position by Executive order. 
December 19, 1912. 
Mr. Thomas E. Price may be promoted from the position of messenger to that of clerk in the Post Office Department without examination. The Postmaster General states that for more than 10 years Mr. Price has been engaged in opening letters in the Division of Dead Letters, and the incessant use of his right Eos has resulted in partial paralysis. He recommends this order, believing that a change in duties will prevent permanent injury. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation. 
December 30, 1912. 
Mr. Samuel E. Fouts may be reinstated as an assistant examiner in the Patent Office, Department of the Interior, without reference to the period of his separation from the service. Mr. Fouts was appointed an assistant examiner through examination on April 6, 1894, and resigned on.September 11, 1899. Since that date he has been actively engaged in the practice of patent law. He attained a high rank as an examiner of ability and efficiency in the Patent Office, and his experience since his separation has given him unusual qualifications for resuming his Patent Office work. The Com- missioner of Patents earnestly desires the reinstatement of Mr. Fouts, and the Secretary of the Interior believes his reinstatement would be of distinct benefit to the service. The supply of eligibles for the position of patent examiner is barely sufficient to meet the needs of the service from year to year. The Civil Service Commission joins in recommending the order. 
December 31, 1912. 
Mr. W. D. Lundy may be appointed to a clerical position without regard to the length of his separation from the service. Mr. Lundy was appointed a clerk in the War Department through the stenographer and typewriter examination on October 1, 1902. He was subsequently transferred to the Treasury Department and resigned on May 6, 1910, as a clerk at $1,400 to become assistant clerk of the Finance Committee of the Senate. He remained in that position until May 1, 1911, when he became personal clerk to Senator Aldrich. On December 12, 1911, he was appointed to a clerical position on the National Monetary Commission, where he WL until the termination of that commission on March 31, 1912; he then resumed his position with Senator Aldrich, which he held until August 18, 1912. 120 THIRTIETH REPORT OF THE U. S. CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION, 
December 19, 1912. 
Mr. Horace P. DeHart may be transferred from the excepted position of confidential 
clerk to the Assistant Secretary of the Interior to an appropriate competitive position in that department. Mr. DeHart has served continuously as confidential clerk for more than nine years to four assistant secretaries. During that period he has acquired a comprehensive knowledge of the varied business assigned to the assistant secretary, which includes numerous Indian matters, including contracts and bonds, leases, heirship cases, petitions for the approval of sale, etc., appeals in land cases, pension appeals, business 
relating to .eleemosynary institutions, expense and transportation accounts, and many miscellaneous items. His practical experience has made him a useful, efficient and well-trained clerk, and according to the Secretary of the Interior his retention in the service will contribute effectively to the despatch of important business. In view of the proved capacity and exceptional qualifications of Mr. DeHart, the Civil Service Commission joins in the recommendation for his transfer to a competitive position by Executive order. 
December 19, 1912. 
Mr. Thomas E. Price may be promoted from the position of messenger to that of clerk in the Post Office Department without examination. The Postmaster General states that for more than 10 years Mr. Price has been engaged in opening letters in the Division of Dead Letters, and the incessant use of his right Eos has resulted in partial paralysis. He recommends this order, believing that a change in duties will prevent permanent injury. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation. 
December 30, 1912. 
Mr. Samuel E. Fouts may be reinstated as an assistant examiner in the Patent Office, Department of the Interior, without reference to the period of his separation from the service. Mr. Fouts was appointed an assistant examiner through examination on April 6, 1894, and resigned on.September 11, 1899. Since that date he has been actively engaged in the practice of patent law. He attained a high rank as an examiner of ability and efficiency in the Patent Office, and his experience since his separation has given him unusual qualifications for resuming his Patent Office work. The Com- missioner of Patents earnestly desires the reinstatement of Mr. Fouts, and the Secretary of the Interior believes his reinstatement would be of distinct benefit to the service. The supply of eligibles for the position of patent examiner is barely sufficient to meet the needs of the service from year to year. The Civil Service Commission joins in recommending the order.
